title: How much oxygen is in the blood
goal: Calculate arterial O₂ content from haemoglobin, saturation and PO₂, and explain how anaemia and altitude lower it.

steps.title: Saturation is a share, content is an amount
steps.text:
Three numbers describe arterial oxygen, and they are easy to mix up:

| number | what it is | typical, sea level |
|---|---|---|
| PaO₂ | pressure of the O₂ *dissolved* in plasma | about 100 mmHg |
| [SaO₂](g:sao2) | share of haemoglobin sites holding O₂ | about 98% |
| [CaO₂](g:cao2) | mL of O₂ actually carried per litre of blood | about 200 mL·L⁻¹ |

Muscles are supplied with an *amount* of O₂, so for delivery content is the one that counts. And content depends on how much haemoglobin there is, which neither PaO₂ nor SaO₂ shows. With [anaemia](g:anaemia), PaO₂ and SaO₂ can be normal while content is low [[c:pao2-anaemia]].

claims.text: PaO₂ and SaO₂ don't show how much O₂ the blood carries; CaO₂ does, and PaO₂ can stay normal in anaemia.

evidence.quote: PaO 2 and the SaO 2 do not provide information on the number of oxygen molecules in the blood.
Since PaO 2 depends on dissolved oxygen, PaO 2 may remain normal in the presence of anemia.

steps.title: The content equation
steps.text:
Add up the O₂ bound to haemoglobin and the O₂ dissolved in plasma [[c:cont-formula]]:

**CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂**

with CaO₂ in **mL O₂ per dL** of blood, Hb in **g·dL⁻¹**, SaO₂ as a **fraction** (0.98, not 98) and PaO₂ in **mmHg**. Multiply by 10 for mL·L⁻¹.

- **1.34**: mL of O₂ one gram of haemoglobin can bind. Some papers use 1.39.
- **0.003**: mL of O₂ dissolved per dL per mmHg (0.03 per litre).

The dissolved part is tiny. Haemoglobin lets blood carry about **70 times** more O₂ than plasma alone could [[c:hb-70fold]].

claims.text: Arterial O₂ content is haemoglobin-bound O₂ plus dissolved O₂: CaO₂ = (Hb × 1.34 × SaO₂) + (0.0031 × PaO₂); the dissolved part is normally minimal.

evidence.quote: It is calculated by the following equation: CaO 2 = (Hgb × 1.34 × SaO 2 ) + (0.0031 × PaO 2 ).
The contribution of the dissolved oxygen to CaO 2 is normally minimal.
Blood O 2 content e .g ., CaO 2 = 1.39 × Hb × SO 2 + 0.003 × PO 2

claims.text: Only about 0.03 mL O₂ per L per mmHg dissolves in blood, while 1 g of Hb binds about 1.34 mL, so haemoglobin raises O₂ carriage about 70-fold.

evidence.quote: Whereas only 0.03 ml O2 * L−1 * mmHg−1 PO2 at 37°C can be transported in blood in physical solution, one gram of Hb can bind ~1.34 ml of O2. Thus, the presence of a normal amount of Hb per volume of blood increases the amount of O2 that can be transported about 70-fold

steps.title: Content of one cyclist's arterial blood
steps.problem: A cyclist at rest has Hb 15 g·dL⁻¹, SaO₂ 98% and PaO₂ 100 mmHg. What is his CaO₂?
steps: Bound O₂ = 1.34 × 15 × 0.98 = 19.7 mL·dL⁻¹. (SaO₂ goes in as 0.98, not 98.)
The dissolved part is 0.3 ÷ 20.0 = 1.5% of the total: in quick estimates you can leave it out.

steps.title: Anaemia: same saturation, less oxygen
steps.text:
Content scales with haemoglobin. Halve the Hb and you halve the content, while saturation and PO₂ hardly change [[c:anaemia-halves]].

A milder case, with SaO₂ 98% and PaO₂ 100 mmHg:

| Hb (g·dL⁻¹) | CaO₂ (mL·dL⁻¹) |
|---|---|
| 15 | 20.0 |
| 12 | 16.1 |

A fifth less haemoglobin, a fifth less O₂ in every litre of blood, and a pulse oximeter would still read 98%. To deliver the same O₂, the heart must pump a quarter more blood (1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25), and at maximal effort it can't.

One catch for athletes: a low Hb *concentration* can also come from extra plasma, with no loss of haemoglobin. That is the next-but-one lesson.

claims.text: Halving haemoglobin concentration halves arterial O₂ content with little or no change in saturation or PO₂.

evidence.quote: In simple terms, a reduction of haemoglobin concentration to half of the normal value is accompanied by a similar reduction in arterial oxygen content with no (or very little) change in % saturation or P

steps.title: Altitude: same haemoglobin, lower saturation
steps.text:
At altitude the air's PO₂ is lower, so arterial PO₂ and SaO₂ fall, and content falls with them even though haemoglobin hasn't changed.

In 8 endurance athletes tested in a chamber, saturation at the end of a VO₂max test fell from 89% at 300 m to 76.5% at 2,800 m. VO₂max fell in a straight line, about **6.3% per 1,000 m**, and was already lower at 800 m than at 300 m [[c:altitude-vo2max]].

With Hb 15 g·dL⁻¹, Hb-bound O₂ at those saturations is 1.34 × 15 × 0.89 = 17.9 versus 1.34 × 15 × 0.765 = 15.4 mL·dL⁻¹: 14% less.

Even at sea level, hard exercise lowers arterial saturation a little, from about 97.5% to about 95% [[c:exercise-desat]].

claims.text: In endurance-trained athletes acutely exposed to simulated altitude, VO₂max fell linearly by about 6.3% per 1,000 m from 300 to 2,800 m, and saturation at the end of the test fell from 89.0% to 76.5%.

evidence.quote: VO(2max) declined linearly from 66+/-1.6 ml kg(-1) min(-1) at 300 m to 55+/-1.6 ml kg(-1) min(-1) at 2,800 m corresponding to a 6.3% decrease per 1,000 m increasing altitude (range 4.6-7.5%).
Arterial haemoglobin oxygen saturation at test cessation (SpO(2min)) declined from 89.0+/-2.9% at 300 m to 76.5+/-4.0% at 2,800 m (P=0.001).

claims.text: At sea level, the lower Hb–O₂ affinity in hard exercise lowers arterial saturation from about 97.5% at rest to about 95%.

evidence.quote: This decrease in Hb-O2 affinity impairs arterial O2 loading and decreases arterial SO2 from ~97.5% at rest to ~95% during high intensity exercise.

points: PaO₂ is a pressure, SaO₂ a share, CaO₂ an amount; muscles need the amount.
CaO₂ (mL·dL⁻¹) = 1.34 × Hb (g·dL⁻¹) × SaO₂ (fraction) + 0.003 × PaO₂ (mmHg): about 20 mL·dL⁻¹, or 200 mL·L⁻¹, at sea level.
The dissolved part is about 1.5% of the total; haemoglobin carries the rest.
Anaemia lowers content in proportion to Hb while saturation and PO₂ stay normal, so a pulse oximeter can't see it.
Altitude lowers saturation and content with the same Hb; VO₂max fell about 6.3% per 1,000 m in acute exposure.

variants.stem: Two cyclists both have an arterial saturation of 98%. Rider A's haemoglobin is 15 g·dL⁻¹, rider B's is 12 g·dL⁻¹. Which statement is right?

options.text: A's blood carries about a quarter more O₂ per litre
options.why: Right: same saturation, but content scales with Hb: 15 ÷ 12 = 1.25.

options.text: Both carry the same O₂, since saturation is equal
options.why: Saturation is a share of the sites; with less Hb there are fewer sites to fill.

options.text: B's blood carries more O₂, as its Hb is less crowded
options.why: Less Hb means less O₂; there is no crowding effect on binding.

options.text: You can't tell without their arterial PO₂
options.why: PO₂ adds only a tiny dissolved part; the Hb difference decides it.

variants.stem: Two runners have the same arterial PO₂ (100 mmHg) and saturation (98%). One has Hb 16 g·dL⁻¹, the other 13.5 g·dL⁻¹. What differs between their arterial blood?

options.text: Its O₂ content: about 18% more in the first
options.why: Right: content ∝ Hb at equal saturation; 16 ÷ 13.5 = 1.19.

options.text: Nothing: equal PO₂ and saturation mean equal oxygen
options.why: Equal PO₂ and saturation hide different amounts of Hb, so different content.

options.text: The second's PO₂ must really be lower
options.why: PO₂ reflects dissolved O₂ and stays normal with less Hb.

options.text: The first's saturation must really be higher
options.why: Saturation is a share of sites; it doesn't depend on how many sites there are.

variants.stem: In a sports lab you often see CaO₂ estimated as 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ alone. Why can the 0.003 × PaO₂ term usually be left out?

options.text: Dissolved O₂ is only about 1.5% of the total
options.why: Right: 0.3 of about 20 mL·dL⁻¹ at a PaO₂ of 100 mmHg.

options.text: Dissolved O₂ can't reach the muscle
options.why: Dissolved O₂ is the form that actually diffuses into tissue; it is just a small amount.

options.text: PaO₂ is always the same, so the term cancels
options.why: PaO₂ varies (exercise, altitude), but the term stays small either way.

options.text: The 1.34 factor already includes the dissolved O₂
options.why: 1.34 is O₂ bound per gram of Hb; the dissolved part is separate.

variants.stem: A triathlete has Hb 14 g·dL⁻¹, SaO₂ 97% and PaO₂ 95 mmHg. What is her CaO₂, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: This leaves out 1.34: it multiplies grams of Hb by saturation, not mL of O₂.
This uses 0.03 for the dissolved term, the per-litre value, in a per-dL equation.
This puts saturation in as 97 instead of 0.97.

variants.stem: A cyclist has Hb 16 g·dL⁻¹, SaO₂ 96% and PaO₂ 90 mmHg. What is his CaO₂, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: This leaves out 1.34: it multiplies grams of Hb by saturation, not mL of O₂.
This uses 0.03 for the dissolved term, the per-litre value, in a per-dL equation.
This puts saturation in as 96 instead of 0.96.

variants.stem: A runner has Hb 13 g·dL⁻¹, SaO₂ 98% and PaO₂ 100 mmHg. What is her CaO₂, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: This leaves out 1.34: it multiplies grams of Hb by saturation, not mL of O₂.
This uses 0.03 for the dissolved term, the per-litre value, in a per-dL equation.
This puts saturation in as 98 instead of 0.98.

variants.stem: A runner with iron deficiency drops from Hb 14 to 11 g·dL⁻¹. SaO₂ stays 98% and PaO₂ 100 mmHg. What is her CaO₂ now, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: Right: 1.34 × 11 × 0.98 = 14.4, plus 0.3 dissolved: 14.7 mL·dL⁻¹, down from 18.7.
That is her old value: it assumes content stays put because saturation did.
This leaves out 1.34: 11 × 0.98 + 0.3.
This puts saturation in as 98 instead of 0.98.

variants.stem: A cyclist's Hb falls from 15 to 12.5 g·dL⁻¹ after a stomach bleed. SaO₂ stays 97% and PaO₂ 95 mmHg. What is his CaO₂ now, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: Right: 1.34 × 12.5 × 0.97 = 16.2, plus 0.3 dissolved: 16.5 mL·dL⁻¹, down from 19.8.
That is his old value: it assumes content stays put because saturation did.
This leaves out 1.34: 12.5 × 0.97 + 0.3.
This puts saturation in as 97 instead of 0.97.

variants.stem: A tired marathoner has Hb 11 g·dL⁻¹ and a finger pulse oximeter reading of 98%. She says her blood oxygen must be fine. Best reply?

options.text: Saturation is normal, but her blood carries less O₂ per litre
options.why: Right: content scales with Hb; saturation is a share of the sites and can't show a shortage of Hb.

options.text: She's right: 98% saturation means normal oxygen delivery
options.why: Delivery depends on content and blood flow; 98% of too little Hb is still too little O₂.

options.text: The oximeter must be wrong: anaemia lowers saturation
options.why: Anaemia leaves saturation and PO₂ nearly unchanged.

options.text: Her PO₂ must be low, which the oximeter misses
options.why: PO₂ reflects dissolved O₂ and stays normal in anaemia.

variants.stem: A triathlete with Hb 14 g·dL⁻¹ has SaO₂ 97% at sea level and 90% on arrival at altitude. Ignoring dissolved O₂, what is her Hb-bound O₂ at altitude, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: Right: 1.34 × 14 × 0.90 = 16.9, down from 18.2 at sea level.
That is her sea-level value: same Hb doesn't mean same content when saturation falls.
This leaves out 1.34: 14 × 0.90.
This puts saturation in as 90 instead of 0.90.

variants.solution: Altitude: 1.34 × 14 × 0.90 = 16.9 mL·dL⁻¹. Sea level: 1.34 × 14 × 0.97 = 18.2. A 7% fall with no change in Hb.

variants.stem: At the end of a VO₂max test at altitude, a runner with Hb 15.5 g·dL⁻¹ is 85% saturated. Ignoring dissolved O₂, what is his Hb-bound O₂, in mL·dL⁻¹?

options.why: This leaves out saturation: 1.34 × 15.5 assumes every site is full.
This leaves out 1.34: 15.5 × 0.85.
This puts saturation in as 85 instead of 0.85.

variants.stem: A cyclist's VO₂max is 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ at 300 m. Using a linear fall of 6.3% per 1,000 m above 300 m, what would you expect at a 1,800 m race?

options.text: About 63
About 66
options.why: This takes off only one 6.3% step; 1,800 m is 1,500 m above the baseline.

options.text: About 62
options.why: This counts 1,800 m from sea level (1.8 × 6.3%) instead of from the 300 m baseline.

options.text: About 70: no loss below 2,000 m
options.why: VO₂max was already lower at 800 m than at 300 m.

variants.stem: A runner's VO₂max is 60 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ at 300 m. Using a linear fall of 6.3% per 1,000 m above 300 m, what would you expect at 2,300 m?

options.text: About 52
About 56
options.why: This takes off only one 6.3% step; 2,300 m is 2,000 m above the baseline.

options.text: About 51
options.why: This counts 2,300 m from sea level (2.3 × 6.3%) instead of from the 300 m baseline.

options.text: About 60: altitude lowers saturation, not VO₂max
options.why: Lower saturation means less O₂ per litre of blood, and VO₂max falls with it.

variants.stem: At rest at sea level, a cyclist with Hb 15 g·dL⁻¹ switches from air (PaO₂ 100 mmHg, SaO₂ 98%) to pure O₂ (PaO₂ 500 mmHg, SaO₂ 100%). Where does most of the extra O₂ content come from?

options.text: Dissolved O₂: +1.2 mL·dL⁻¹ versus +0.4 bound
options.why: Right: 0.003 × 400 = 1.2 dissolved; 1.34 × 15 × 0.02 = 0.4 bound, as Hb was nearly full already.

options.text: Bound O₂: saturation rises a lot with pure O₂
options.why: Saturation can only go from 98% to 100%: Hb was already almost full.

options.text: Neither: content can't rise above 20 mL·dL⁻¹
options.why: It rises a little, by about 1.6 mL·dL⁻¹, mostly as dissolved O₂.

options.text: Bound O₂: the 1.34 factor rises with PaO₂
options.why: 1.34 is fixed by haemoglobin's chemistry; it doesn't change with PO₂.

variants.solution: Bound: 1.34 × 15 × (1.00 − 0.98) = 0.4 mL·dL⁻¹. Dissolved: 0.003 × (500 − 100) = 1.2 mL·dL⁻¹. Total gain 1.6 mL·dL⁻¹, about 8%.

variants.stem: A study of 8 endurance athletes found VO₂max fell 6.3% per 1,000 m in a hypobaric chamber, each altitude tested on arrival. A coach applies it to a team after 3 weeks living at 1,800 m. What most limits that use?

options.text: It tested acute exposure; weeks at altitude bring acclimatisation
options.why: Right: acute tests can't show how acclimatisation (more ventilation, more red cells) changes the loss.

options.text: A chamber can't lower PO₂ the way real altitude does
options.why: A hypobaric chamber lowers air pressure, which is what real altitude does.

options.text: VO₂max can't be measured accurately at altitude
options.why: Douglas bags measure VO₂ fine at altitude; that isn't the main issue.

options.text: Eight athletes is too few to see any effect
options.why: The effect was large and consistent; small n limits precision, not detection here.
